\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Serving multimodal RAG at scale is a GPU provisioning problem with two levers: routing reduces generation compute
per query, and index placement handles visual-index memory as the corpus grows. Measured end to
end with real retrieval and generation on one GPU, the content-aware router CAVR-CE uses 29\% less GPU compute
than always combining text and image contexts, at a mean ANLS cost of 0.008; against a quality-blind mix
of the visual and hybrid paths at equal ANLS it saves 20\%. In a load test simulated from
measured service times, it reduces the GPUs needed for 100 queries/s at p95 $\le$ 2\,s from 106 to
72, while always using the page image alone needs 64 at lower ANLS. Its cost
weight is set at serving time; confidence-based escalation reached the same operating point as lowering this
weight.

On two multi-GPU nodes (three Tesla P40 and two NVIDIA A10 GPUs), sharding the visual index
holds exhaustive search at constant latency as the corpus grows with the number of GPUs, with parallel efficiency
of at least 99.6\% and 97.6\% from 50k pages up. With the index in host memory,
two GPUs searched a million pages in large batches at close to the throughput per GPU of GPU-resident search,
which would need 16 GPUs; the price is single-query latency (6.4\,s), which limits this
placement to batch search.

The evaluation also shows what does not hold. Keyword-derived route labels do not reflect which path
answers correctly, cost estimates from list prices do not match measured costs, and with a shared generator the text path is
not a cheap path. A per-query oracle (ANLS 0.630 at 0.486 GPU-s) shows how much remains: the
bottleneck is predicting, before generation, whether a path will succeed.

The routing results come from one GPU and simulated load, and sharding and the host-memory index were measured on
separate server nodes for retrieval only. Future work should validate routing on a multi-GPU cluster with a production serving engine, find an overload signal that lets $\lambda$ follow load, improve per-query success
prediction, and extend routing to queries that contain images.
